articles.title: Hank Brown is officially the Hawkeye QB1 and he’s making it a full-time job
articles.summary: For a long time, being a college football player meant being a student-athlete. Now, as rules change and five years of eligibility is guaranteed, players can...
articles.body:
For a long time, being a college football player meant being a student-athlete. Now, as rules change and five years of eligibility is guaranteed, players can more of their focus to the field. The Iowa Hawkeye's newly announced first-string quarterback is in his fourth year in college. But he's able to put his focus on football, all because of the hard work he put in as an underclassman in the classroom.

"When I was at Auburn, I would take classes in the summer and the way they would do it is you could take classes in the summer so you could lighten your load in the fall," said Brown. "My first few years I would take classes year-round, cause you're there all summer so why not take some classes."

That work at Auburn University transferred over to the University of Iowa. Brown graduated as a Hawkeye last May with a major in enterprise leadership. With two years of college athletic eligibility left, he stays a student as a non-degree seeking student. Meaning a light load of online classes.

Brown's been backing up two quarterbacks who did the same thing. Mark Gronowski last season at Iowa and Peyton Thorne at Auburn. With the extra free time, Brown spends most of it in the film room or the facility. Taking in as much of the complicated offense as he can.

"You got to actually learn your playbook if you want to play in this offense," said Iowa wide receiver Tony Diaz.

Then on top of that Brown studies that week's opposing team. And works to figure out how the Iowa offense can attack it.

"The week moves fast. From Sunday to Wednesday night is kind of our workdays and busy days to be able to pack everything in, you got to be on your P's and Q's," said Brown.

Of course, it's not a one-man job for Brown. He spends a lot of time with the Iowa offensive coordinator Tim Lester and his staff. They work through the gameplan each week. Those sessions are where Brown is able to learn and soak in the most knowledge.

"Why a play is in for this, and I get to see them kind of break it down," said Brown.

Brown's preparation each week adds to endless hours. Almost like he's working overtime at his profession, which at this point, it basically is.

"College football is almost becoming like a job at this point," said Brown. "It's getting closer and closer to the NFL at this point."

That prep is important, and the more time Brown is able to spend, the more comfortable he feels during the game. It's why in moments like the final offensive drive for the Hawkeyes in the CyHawk game, he was able to guide the team down to field goal range.

"He was just saying stay calm. He's a great leader," said Diaz after the game. "Any time he talks, you feel good."

With a top 20 opponent awaiting the Hawkeyes on Saturday, that prep will be key. Especially since the game is at Michigan, in the Big House.

"(Brown's) probably the most critical because he plays the position that impacts a lot of things and has got a lot on his plate," said Iowa head coach Kirk Ferentz. "But yeah, one thing about playing in this conference, you're going to be in a really tough environment this week."

Brown's first official game as the first-string quarterback is Saturday at Michigan. That game kicks off at 2:30 pm central time on CBS 4.

Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Davante Adams had quite the performance in the club's 28-6 Monday night win over the New York Giants . He hauled in eight receptions off 10 targets for 195 yards and two touchdowns, which translated to 41.5 fantasy points in traditional PPR scoring leagues. But is that type of production sustainable?

ESPN's fantasy football expert Field Yates broke down the 33-year-old's performance in "Monday Night Football" in the latest segment of "Fantasy Focus." Yates was impressed with Adams' play and liked how involved the Rams star was outside of just red zone usage. Puka Nacua 's absence certainly played a part, and Yates ponders whether fantasy players will need the four-year veteran to miss games for Adams to put up big numbers. But he seems to like Adams' outlook regardless.

"Last night was, to me, more important than what we saw last season from Davante Adams , in the sense that Davante Adams last year, and you still get the fantasy points, it's not how, it's how many you get," Yates said. As the Texas football program recorded a 30-6 win over UTSA last Saturday, the talk around the team centered on a situation with head coach Steve Sarkisian , quarterback Arch Manning , and ESPN reporter Holly Rowe. While the controversy around the Texas football team is in the rearview mirror, Arch's uncle, Eli Manning , would give his thoughts on what went down.

To refresh, after Sarkisian walked off and avoided a post-game interview with Rowe after the Longhorns' 24-23 win over the Ohio State Buckeyes on Sept. 12, an artificial intelligence (AI) video circulated of Sarkisian striking Rowe in that same scenario. Manning would bring up the fake video in a press conference, calling it "hilarious," which inevitably led to an apology to Rowe.

Eli Manning has advice for Texas football 's Arch Manning

Eli Manning spoke with Front Office Sports (FOC) about the matter and was asked if he reached out to his nephew about the situation, offering a piece of advice.

"I didn't reach out after that one. Reached out after the Ohio State game and just said proud of him, hanging in there, tough, wasn't easy to start the game, but he stayed patient…most of my advice, more football stuff. He'll have to figure out that media on his own, and a lot of it is just kind of growing pains," Manning said.

"You feel like they're your pal, you relax with them a little bit, you try to be funny, and then they can take it and run," Manning continued. "So you just gotta you gotta be careful. You gotta find your moments where you can be funny, you can be relaxed, but there's certain things that you know you just gotta learn and deal with it. articles.title: Tuesday Seacoast Standout: Portsmouth girls soccer senior captain delivers in clutch
articles.summary: Portsmouth senior captain Piper Hindle scored the game-winning goal in Tuesday's 2-1 win over Concord, and was named Seacoast Standout Athlete of the Day.
articles.body:
CONCORD - After senior defender Piper Hindle scored the game-winning goal in Portsmouth High School's 2-1 girls soccer victory over Concord on Tuesday, Sept. 22, coach Rick Hugener praised the unlikely source of offense.

"That's her first goal of the year," Hugener said. "She plays left back, so she's a defender. We were pressing most of the game, and because we were tied she was pushing higher up the field late. She got the ball about 25 yards out and ripped a shot high to the far side of the goal."

Hindle was named the Seacoast Standout Athlete of the Day.

Hugener said Hindle's goal was especially meaningful given her leadership role.

"It was great," he said. "She's a senior captain and one of our leaders. For her to step up and get a win for us is amazing. She played a great game defensively and was really involved in our transition into the attack."

The Clippers were forced to grind out the win while dealing with injuries that have shuffled players into unfamiliar roles.

"We have a lot of girls playing in different positions than they're normally playing because of injuries," Hugener said. "Just the effort and the grind they showed throughout the game was impressive."

Hugener said Concord's defensive approach made scoring chances difficult to come by.

"We possessed the ball well, but they packed it in most of the game," he said. "It was tough to break through and get quality shots when there were usually nine players behind the ball around the box. We kept pushing, and finally we broke through toward the end of the game, which was nice."

articles.title: Portland State coach explains why he declined Oregon's offer of 10-minute quarters in second half of 84-0 loss
articles.summary: Oregon led 49-0 at halftime as it set a school record for points in a game.
articles.body:
Portland State football coach Chris Fisk has confirmed that his team had no interest in playing less than a full game against Oregon .

The Ducks blew out the FCS-level Vikings 84-0 on Friday night and set a school record for most points in a single game in the modern era. Monday, Oregon coach Dan Lanning said that he had twice asked Portland State if the Vikings wanted to play 10-minute quarters in the second half as Oregon led 49-0 at halftime but that PSU had declined.

Oregon's previous scoring record was 81 points. That came in a 74-point win over Portland State in 2023.

In a statement to the Oregonian on Tuesday, Fisk explained why he didn't want the game shortened. He was hired as Portland State's coach in December after the Vikings went 1-11 in 2025.

"We have a lot of respect for Oregon football and Coach Lanning," Fisk said. "We had been offered 10-minute quarters for both the third and fourth quarters and chose to play the full game. We chose that for the development of our program. We came to play 60 minutes, regardless of the outcome. "Teaching the kids that we don't get to run away from hard things was our intent. Portland State University has nothing but respect for the University of Oregon and their football program. They didn't pay us to come down there and take it easy on us. We're on to Weber State this week and wish the Ducks well against USC."

articles.title: "La gente en España siente que el club le pertenece; no lo comprendí hasta que lo viví en primera persona"
articles.standfirst: Bob Voulgaris, propietario del Castellón, reflexiona en MARCA sobre las diferencias más grandes entre el aficionado deportivo de España y el de Norteamérica
articles.summary: Bob Voulgaris, propietario del Castellón, reflexiona en MARCA sobre las diferencias más grandes entre el aficionado deportivo de España y el de Norteamérica
articles.body: En una entrevista en MARCA, Haralabos Voulgaris, propietario del Castellón, reflexiona sobre las diferencias más grandes que nota entre el aficionado deportivo de España y el de Norteamérica. Antes de llegar a Castalia (julio de 2022), generó una fortuna realizando apuestas en la NBA, lo que posteriormente le llevó a convertirse en director de Investigación y Desarrollo Cuantitativo de los Dallas Mavericks. "Probablemente, la mayor diferencia sea la relación entre el aficionado y el club. En España, el club está profundamente vinculado a la ciudad y, a menudo, a varias generaciones de una misma familia. La gente no sólo anima al equipo; siente que el club le pertenece. Los deportes norteamericanos, en cambio, parecen mucho más comercializados. No se trata sólo del partido en sí, sino de todo lo que se puede vender al aficionado en torno a él. El ejemplo más insidioso, en mi opinión, son las apuestas. Se han integrado tanto en las retransmisiones, la cobertura mediática y la experiencia deportiva en general que, a veces, puede resultar difícil separar el partido del producto de apuestas que lo rodea. También se observa una mayor atención en las valoraciones de las franquicias, los derechos de retransmisión, los grupos propietarios y el capital riesgo", explica. Bob sostiene que el fútbol español todavía parece menos dominado por todas esas cosas: "Existe una mayor sensación de que el club representa un lugar, una historia y una comunidad. Cuando el Castellón gana o pierde, se puede sentir de verdad cómo cambia el ambiente de la ciudad. Eso era algo que entendía intelectualmente antes de venir aquí, pero que realmente no se comprende hasta que se vive en primera persona".

articles.body: Una derrota en un partido tan trascendental como un derbi bien vale para sacar a relucir las miserias del perdedor. En este caso, le tocó al Real Madrid. Apenas 24 horas después de caer 2-1 contra el Atleti, empezó a circular el dato de que es el equipo que menos corre de LaLiga. Un titular fácil de repetir y, a la vez, fácil de simplificar demasiado. Importa más la velocidad a la que un equipo cubre el campo que el total de terreno que recorre. El Barcelona, líder de LaLiga, es la prueba más clara de esa idea. Porque medir el fútbol solo en kilómetros es quedarse a medias. Un equipo puede completar la misma distancia trotando en bloque que otro corriendo a máxima velocidad en cada transición, y el marcador de distancia total no distingue entre ambas cosas. Es un caso muy extremo, pero podría darse. La distancia total de un equipo suma de todo: trotes de vuelta tras una pérdida, desplazamientos sin presión, y también los esprints que deciden un partido. Los datos dividen ese recorrido en franjas de velocidad, y ahí aparecen las dos categorías que de verdad interesan: la carrera de alta intensidad o HSR, entre 19,8 y 25,2 km/h, y el esprint, a partir de 25,2 km/h. Así, al menos, los clasifica Driblab, aunque no difieren mucho de otras compañías de datos. Son los metros que un futbolista corre cuando presiona una salida de balón, se desmarca al espacio o persigue una pérdida en campo contrario. El resto es, en buena parte, kilometraje neutro. Decir que el Madrid no corre ya es un término mal usado. ¿Qué es correr? Porque si lo que queremos es decir cuánta distancia ha recorrido hablamos de carreras y tramos andando o trotando. Por tanto, lo que habría que apuntar es que el Madrid hace menos distancia que otros. Y sí, en distancia total, el Madrid firma 104,3 km de media por partido y cierra la tabla, el más bajo de los veinte equipos de LaLiga. 104,3 km y no 84 km , como se ha visto reflejado en otras informaciones. "Es muy raro que un equipo al completo cubra una distancia inferior a los 100km en un partido", explica a MARCA un preparador físico de un equipo de Primera división. El patrón se repite en la distancia de alta intensidad, 4.975,5 metros por partido, también el último puesto, y en el número de acciones a ese ritmo, 338,5, otra vez el farolillo rojo. Tres clasificaciones, tres últimos puestos. El matiz aparece en el esprint. Ahí el Madrid ya no ocupa la última plaza: son 2.248 metros por partido, la undécima marca de la Liga, prácticamente la media. El equipo de Mourinho esprinta a un ritmo cercano al del resto de LaLiga; el problema aparece antes, en el volumen general y, sobre todo, en la carrera de alta intensidad, la franja que más veces conecta con una recuperación, un desmarque o una presión bien realizada. El Barcelona lleva la idea al extremo contrario, y es aquí donde el argumento se refuerza de verdad. El líder de LaLiga cubre 108,6 km por partido, el 16º registro de la competición, ni siquiera entre los diez equipos que más corren. Un candidato al título y un equipo que arrastra un arranque discreto de temporada pueden compartir, sorprendentemente, la mitad baja de la tabla de kilometraje. Lo que los separa aparece en la franja de velocidad donde se ejecuta ese esfuerzo. En distancia HSR el Barcelona sube hasta la sexta posición, con 5.858,8 metros por partido, casi 900 más que el conjunto blanco. En número de acciones a esa velocidad es tercero, con 413,4. Y en esprints aparece la cifra que mejor resume el argumento: 132,4 por partido, la más alta de LaLiga, muy lejos de los 78,8 de Osasuna, el equipo que menos esprinta de la competición. Ese salto entre un discreto 16º puesto en distancia total y el liderato en esprints explica, en parte, por qué el Barcelona manda en la clasificación mientras el Madrid firma el peor registro de alta intensidad de toda LaLiga. La tabla de kilómetros y la tabla de puntos no siempre coinciden; la de los esfuerzos a máxima velocidad se parece mucho más a esta última.

articles.title: Football scouting: Hidden gems and the race to discover emerging talent
articles.summary: Through live scouting and increasing data and footage, top clubs now have tabs on a large proportion of the world's talent.
articles.body:
The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez.

"When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.

Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.

It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.

Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment.

"We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting.

"And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."

From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered.

"That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any more in football," says Kjaer. "Sometimes it does, but it's rare."

"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.

Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.

It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.

Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.

The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI.

"The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."

Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.

The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'.

"There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."

Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience.

"We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club.

"Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."

"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer.

"I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play.

"When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."

One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".

Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.

For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.

Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.

As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in.

Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets.

"They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."

Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities.

"It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner.

"We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."

One of those markets continues to be Africa.

"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.

Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments.

"We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph.

With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.

But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities.

"Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria.

"The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."

Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.

Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches.

"One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her.

"Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."

Some Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.

Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time.

"The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."

Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.

The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.

It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.

Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.

Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.

Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on.

"I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer.

"We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment.

"What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."

There remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.

A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group.

"Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players.

"Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."

Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.

Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.

Other Eyeball , external partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain.

"Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner.

"A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18.

"There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

articles.title: Miguel Morrás, el 'heredero de Indurain' que fue el primer arcoíris español: "Que Noval sea tranquilo"
articles.standfirst: Dejó el fútbol, conquistó el arcoíris júnior y España vio en él al heredero de Miguelón, pero su carrera se apagó casi sin empezar; treinta años después, habla con MARCA y celebra que Benjamín Noval se sume a ese club minúsculo de españoles que fueron campeones del mundo siendo casi niños
articles.summary: Dejó el fútbol, conquistó el arcoíris júnior y España vio en él al heredero de Miguelón, pero su carrera se apagó casi sin empezar; treinta años después, habla con MARCA y celebra que Benjamín Noval se sume a ese club minúsculo de españoles que fueron campeones del mundo siendo casi niños
articles.body: Miguel Morrás tenía 18 años cuando descubrió que se puede llegar demasiado pronto a todas partes. Había dejado el fútbol, había descubierto la bicicleta, y ya vestía el maillot arcoíris. En Quito, en 1994, se escapó durante 42 kilómetros para ganar el Mundial júnior, con un ataque 'a lo Remco' cuyos detalles aún perduran vivos en su memoria. Detrás quedó el pelotón, deshecho; delante, de golpe, apareció una vida que todos parecían tener ya escrita para él. Era navarro en los años de Miguel Induráin, y bastó ese parentesco geográfico, sumado a una victoria tan rotunda, para que las comparaciones echaran a correr más deprisa que el propio Morrás. España buscaba herederos para su gran campeón y acababa de tropezarse con un muchacho que ganaba solo, sin necesitar a nadie. "Estaba la similitud de que los dos éramos navarros, y eso hizo que tuviese quizá un poquito más de bombo", recuerda ahora, treinta y dos años después, en conversación con MARCA el hasta el martes único español campeón del mundo junior (el único aún en ruta porque el reciente éxito de Benja Noval es en la crono). Morrás intenta quitarle importancia a lo que hizo entonces. Sabe que aquel verano cambió su nombre para siempre, aunque no del modo en que él lo había imaginado. "Para mí, Induráin es el deportista que más alegrías me ha dado", confiesa, y en esa frase cabe algo parecido a la devoción. El ídolo y el joven campeón pertenecían al mismo territorio, casi al mismo paisaje, pero sus carreras acabarían siguiendo caminos opuestos: una pareció no terminar nunca; la otra apenas tuvo tiempo de comenzar. Antes de ser ciclista, Morrás había probado casi todos los deportes que se le pusieron por delante. Vivió de niño en Francia, jugó allí al fútbol y siguió haciéndolo al volver a Navarra. En el Izarra destacó lo suficiente como para llamar la atención del Athletic, y llegó a medirse, balón por medio, con futbolistas como Guti e Iván de la Peña en categorías inferiores. Tenía piernas y tenía instinto para seguir persiguiendo esa pelota. Eligió, sin embargo, una bicicleta. En 1993 empezó a competir con el Club Ciclista Estella. El cambio fue tan brusco como natural pareció después, ya sobre la carretera. Según contó él mismo años más tarde a MARCA, llegó a ganar carreras sin apenas entrenar, como si el talento le sobrara antes de que le hiciera falta el esfuerzo. En categoría júnior venció en 32 de sus 64 participaciones. No esperaba al esprint: atacaba, se marchaba, y obligaba a los demás a ir asumiendo, kilómetro a kilómetro, una derrota que todavía tardaría en hacerse oficial. Quito vino a confirmar que aquel dominio no conocía fronteras: Morrás atacó en el Mundial y convirtió la fuga en una larga, interminable afirmación de todo lo que podía llegar a ser. La victoria le abrió las puertas del Banesto aficionado. En 1995 siguió destacando y, al año siguiente, firmó por la ONCE de Manolo Saiz sin haber cumplido aún los 20 años. El equipo reunía a figuras ya consagradas, y el recién llegado tenía por delante cuatro temporadas para crecer a su sombra. Sobre el papel, aquello era una oportunidad inmensa. Morrás cree hoy que fue, también, un salto dado demasiado pronto. "Yo venía de muy pocos años de andar en bicicleta. A los tres o cuatro años de empezar, ya me estaba convirtiendo en profesional", explica a MARCA. Le faltaba experiencia para conocer sus propios límites, y quizá le faltó tiempo, sobre todo, para que el cuerpo aprendiera a sostener lo que se le pedía. "Pasar tan pronto a profesionales creo que me perjudicó. Era otra época: entonces costaba más años llegar arriba". La rodilla empezó a dolerle sin avisar demasiado. Después vinieron las consultas médicas, los intentos de encontrar una solución, los meses en los que entrenar dejó de ser una promesa y se convirtió en un problema diario. El muchacho que había sido capaz de marcharse de un pelotón entero ya no conseguía avanzar. "Una de las rodillas dijo que no podía seguir. En aquella época no se pudo recuperar. Quizá hoy, con los métodos que hay, habría sido diferente", reflexiona, con la calma de quien ha repasado la misma frase muchas veces. Recuerda que se puso en manos del doctor Guillén, y que tampoco allí encontraron la manera de enderezar su caso. Su pasado como futbolista reaparecía una y otra vez entre las explicaciones posibles. Habla de la musculatura que había desarrollado antes de dedicarse al ciclismo, y de unas piernas arqueadas que, cree, pudieron pasarle factura. No presenta aquellas sospechas como un diagnóstico cerrado, sino como una hipótesis con la que ha aprendido a convivir. Lo que sí tiene claro es el resultado: mientras otros corredores de su generación empezaban a levantar, ladrillo a ladrillo, una carrera profesional, él iba viendo cómo se le escapaba, sin ruido, la posibilidad de construir la suya. Entonces volvió la mirada hacia los estudios. "Empecé a centrarme en la universidad", cuenta. Acabaría encontrando una carrera en las finanzas que lo llevó por plazas tan distintas como Wall Street, Londres y Singapur. Le gustaban los números, la estadística, la rapidez con la que hay que decidir bajo presión, casi como si aquella tensión le recordara, de otra manera, a la carretera. Su segunda vida le ofreció retos, viajes, satisfacciones. Nunca ha necesitado fingir que le fue mal para admitir, al mismo tiempo, que perdió algo importante por el camino. Morrás no vive de espaldas al ciclismo actual, ni mucho menos. Lo sigue con la mirada de quien entiende de qué está hablando. "El ciclismo está pasando una época dorada", afirma. Multinacionales cada vez más implicadas, mejoras constantes en entrenamiento y en tecnología, en bicicletas y en ruedas: para él, las velocidades que se ven hoy en carrera son la suma de todo eso. "Si repites lo del año anterior, estás perdido. Todos los años tienes que mejorar", resume, y pone como ejemplo a Pogačar y a Vingegaard, capaces de llegar cada temporada todavía más rápidos. Cita también a Van der Poel -"haciendo lo que hace"- y a Pidcock, "que se atreve a hacer cosas diferentes", como prueba de que el nivel se ha disparado en varias direcciones a la vez. "Es algo que nunca habíamos visto: un corredor que compite en distintas especialidades, campeón olímpico, capaz de ganar una crono en una vuelta y también la Milán-San Remo. Pueden hacer podio en LaVuelta, ganar una Sanremo y también sacar medalla en MTB", reflexiona. Y añade, sin nostalgia forzada, que eso es precisamente lo que a él le habría gustado tocar: "En mi época se cuidaba mucho el detalle, yo era curioso y meticuloso, pero no existía el conocimiento que hay ahora". Hoy, ya alejado de las carreteras, reparte su tiempo entre las finanzas y Dubái, ciudad a la que se mudó hace dos años y donde ejerce como portfolio manager. "Yo lo he echado en falta", dice cuando se le pregunta por el ciclismo. Morrás explica que su sueño era estar en verano, sobre la bicicleta, mientras la gente seguía las grandes carreras desde la carretera o desde el sofá. "Por suerte he vivido otras experiencias que han sido muy enriquecedoras", añade enseguida, como si no quisiera dejar la frase anterior sola demasiado tiempo. Las dos ideas conviven en la misma vida: agradecer lo que vino después, y seguir pensando, de vez en cuando, en lo que pudo haber sido. Durante años, su historia ha reaparecido cada vez que un joven español gana antes de tiempo. Ya ocurrió con Juan Ayuso. Antes de este Mundial, Morrás miraba ya con especial interés a Benjamín Noval, y reconocía en él algunas condiciones que conoce de memoria: la potencia, la musculatura que viene del fútbol, una aparente facilidad para la contrarreloj que a él mismo, en su día, le sobraba. "Me gusta mucho su perfil. Me gusta cómo le están llevando porque hace también MTB y CX, que son disciplinas importantes. Igual que Del Toro hizo gravel o CX. Con ello aprendes a dominar bien la bici", afirma. El elogio llegaba acompañado de un deseo, casi una súplica disfrazada de frase corta: "Ojalá tenga más suerte que yo". El deseo, de momento, se ha cumplido con creces. Este martes, en Montreal, Noval se colgó el oro en la contrarreloj júnior con un tiempo de 25 minutos y 17 segundos, el primer título mundial español en la historia de esa especialidad y esa categoría. Treinta y dos años después de Quito, Morrás ha dejado de ser el único que sabe, tan joven, lo que pesa un arcoíris sobre los hombros. Ahora tiene, por fin, la compañía que él mismo pidió para el camino de otro. No pretende trasladarle su destino a otro corredor, como si las historias se heredaran igual que un maillot. Las épocas son distintas, y Morrás cree que el ciclismo actual permite a los jóvenes competir antes al máximo nivel. Pero hay una parte de la exigencia que, a su juicio, no ha cambiado: el desgaste se acumula incluso cuando un talento parece capaz de hacerlo todo sin que se le note el esfuerzo. Por eso pide cuidado con el calendario, y en especial con las grandes vueltas. "Tres semanas agotan mucho. Son cuerpos muy jóvenes", advierte. Su consejo para un corredor que empieza en profesionales es sencillo, casi austero: elegir durante un tiempo las carreras menos exigentes y dejar que el cuerpo aprenda a su propio ritmo. "Los dos primeros años deberían tomárselos con mucha tranquilidad". Habla desde una experiencia que no le dio respuestas para salvar su carrera, pero sí le dejó una pregunta que nunca ha terminado de abandonarlo del todo: qué habría ocurrido si alguien, él mismo incluido, hubiera esperado un poco más. Cuando se le pide que imagine una conversación con el Miguel de 18 años, recién proclamado campeón del mundo, no le habla de victorias ni de contratos: "Le diría que se lo tomase todo con mucha tranquilidad". Y vuelve, inevitablemente, a la rodilla: al cuidado que quizá habría debido prestarle, a aquella urgencia que parecía inevitable cuando todos le señalaban ya, con el dedo y con la voz, un futuro brillante. Morrás sigue pendiente del ciclismo español, aunque ya no compita en él. Ve motivos para ilusionarse en las medallas de las categorías inferiores y en los jóvenes que van apareciendo en unos Mundiales cada vez más disputados. "Hay más países competitivos y salen chicos de más lugares", observa alguien feliz del último éxito de Enric Mas en LaVuelta aunque "por desgracia al Movistar se le están escapando algunas de las jóvenes promesas en los últimos tiempos". Quizá por eso cada éxito le parece más valioso que el anterior. Quizá también porque sabe, mejor que nadie, lo difícil que es adivinar qué ocurrirá después de una medalla. Morrás tampoco ve a España entre las favoritas para la prueba élite del domingo. "Los corredores que tenemos ahora en la selección no dan el perfil de especialistas en carreras de un día", explica. Por eso propone correr con paciencia, guardar fuerzas y reservar las cartas para intentar sorprender: "En vez de ir de cara, hay que ir un poquito a robarles la merienda". A su juicio, igualar o mejorar el octavo puesto logrado en Suiza "sería un éxito". La suya llegó en Quito y aún conserva intacta su fuerza, congelada en el tiempo como una fotografía que nadie ha vuelto a revelar. Morrás, el otro Miguel, fue campeón del mundo antes de tener edad para saber cuánto puede cambiar una vida en un solo verano. Treinta y dos años después, el arcoíris júnior español tiene, por fin, un segundo nombre. Y él, cuando mira a quienes vienen detrás, intenta contarles también la parte que aquella fotografía nunca mostró: que llegar pronto es maravilloso, siempre que después te dejen tiempo para quedarte.

articles.body: Luis Milla, futbolista español del Como de Cesc Fábregas, le explicó a Juanma Castaño en el programa 'El Partidazo de COPE' su frustrado fichaje por el Atlético de Madrid de Simeone cuando jugaba en el Getafe. "Fue el último día de mercado, me estaba yendo a jugar al golf, me llamaron y me dijeron que me quería firmar el Atlético de Madrid", contó el futbolista de 31 años sobre una operación que finalmente no cuajó. "No se pudo dar por los tiempos", compartió.

articles.title: Roberto Gómez, sobre Mourinho: "Nadie habla del juego"
articles.standfirst: El colaborador de La Tribu cuestionó la actuación de Ortiz Arias en el derbi y señaló al entrenador del Real Madrid
articles.summary: El colaborador de La Tribu cuestionó la actuación de Ortiz Arias en el derbi y señaló al entrenador del Real Madrid
articles.body: Roberto Gómez analizó junto a Raúl Varela en La Tribu de Radio MARCA la resaca del derbi del Metropolitano y la polémica generada alrededor del arbitraje de Ortiz Arias. El periodista evitó entrar en la batalla de comunicados, aunque sí valoró las principales acciones polémicas del encuentro y puso el foco en el fútbol mostrado sobre el terreno de juego. "No comento comentarios ni comunicados", aseguró Roberto Gómez cuando Raúl Varela llevó la conversación hacia la situación que atraviesa el fútbol español. "No soy especialista en comunicados", insistió. Roberto Gómez sí entró a analizar lo sucedido con Ortiz Arias en el Metropolitano. "El comité de árbitros ha ratificado lo que te expliqué el otro día en las acciones en el Metropolitano", explicó. El periodista fue claro con una de las jugadas más discutidas del encuentro: "Ortiz Arias debió expulsar al coreano. Yo creo que en estos momentos es la jugada de mayor comentario". Además, añadió: "El penalti es claro, la otra cartulina amarilla también es bastante clara". Más allá de las decisiones concretas, Roberto también cuestionó la manera en la que Ortiz Arias dirigió el partido: "La dirección del partido intentó el colegueo. Intentó Kang In para acá, Manu para allá... Y cuando empiezan los árbitros a llamar por el nombre, pues entonces es señal de que no están fuertes". Para Roberto Gómez, sin embargo, la polémica arbitral está provocando que el debate se aleje de lo sucedido futbolísticamente en el derbi. "Pero nadie habla del juego. Las protestas arbitrales siempre vienen por parte de los que pierden", afirmó. El colaborador de La Tribu insistió en esa idea: "Si Madrid hubiese ganado no pasaría nada con Kang In. Nadie habla del juego". Roberto Gómez también puso el foco en José Mourinho y en la reacción posterior al encuentro: "Y desde luego es una manera, la actitud que se tomó por parte, sobre todo de Mourinho, en lugar de hablar del juego, hablar de los árbitros". El periodista cerró el asunto regresando a su negativa a entrar en la guerra de comunicados: "Yo no comento comunicado. No comento comunicado porque ya está bien. Para eso ya están otros".

articles.title: Jurgen Klopp: New Germany manager set to begin reign as boss
articles.summary: As Jurgen Klopp prepares for his first game as Germany manager, BBC Sport looks at how is trying to turn their fortunes around.
articles.body:
It has been quite the ride since Jurgen Klopp was announced as Germany's head coach in July.

In his first news conference, Klopp admonished the media, urging them to treat him fairly and refrain from any attacks against his family.

Last Thursday, during another media conference, Klopp called for "positive patriotism" amid political turmoil in the country.

When asked whether he considers himself an ambassador for Germany in his new role, Klopp's answer was a serious one.

"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us," said Klopp.

"I want it so that when someone waves it, no-one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."

His statement was made in light of the success of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-immigration party has since scored another win in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Klopp's remarks were widely and positively discussed in the media - the German national team represents a diverse Germany, as several players come from a migrant background.

KIopp also remarked about the recent success of Alexander Zverev at the US Open, the women's basketball team at the European Championship and German athletes at the European Athletics Championships, saying sport can ensure "a sense of community".

He added: "This is our mission: we need to create a good atmosphere."

Klopp knows, intentionally or not, how to make headlines.

However, the German Football Association (DFB) didn't hire the former Liverpool boss on an annual salary of £6m to become a commentator on the state of Germany - but to transform a floundering national team.

Klopp wants to 'reclaim' flag amid German elections

Klopp starts Germany reign by threatening to quit

Between the two news conferences, Klopp looked like the busiest national team boss on the planet, making countless visits to league games and training facilities.

One day fans could see Klopp sitting in the stands of Dortmund's Signal Iduna Park, his old stomping ground and, not long after, they may have caught a picture of him in the VIP lounge of Mainz's stadium or somewhere near Eintracht Frankfurt's training pitch talking to players.

Klopp has approached this new job with open eyes. Initially, the charismatic 59-year-old drew up a list of 57 players who could have been selected for this first international break.

"Players will receive chances who don't even expect it yet," Klopp said in July.

His first selection wasn't short of surprises. In the flavour of a trial-and-error principle, Klopp and his staff decided to select two almost completely different squads for the upcoming four games.

The first squad, including Joshua Kimmich, Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala, will face arch-rivals the Netherlands at Johan Cruyff Arena on Thursday (19:45 BST) and host Greece on Sunday.

The second squad, with Florian Wirtz and Aleksandar Pavlovic, face Serbia at home and Greece on the road in the second half of this international break. The only player who was selected for both is back-up goalkeeper Finn Dahmen.

The selection process means we will not see Germany's best starting XI this time around. Instead, Klopp clearly intends to try out new players, some of whom played in Germany's second tier only a few months ago.

Take, for example, Felix Keidel, a 23-year-old full-back-midfielder hybrid from recently promoted SV Elversberg.

A year ago, Keidel was as far away from the national team as the Oktoberfest from Rio Carnival.

Now Keidel - just like Mika Baur, Bambase Conte, Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu, and Vitaly Janelt - has the chance to show he could be a valuable cog in the machine.

Klopp has never built his success merely on star names - he has always taken a liking to undervalued and overlooked players.

He once signed an little-known Polish winger by the name of Lukasz Piszczek and moulded him into one of the best right-backs in Europe who would go toe-to-toe with Cristiano Ronaldo in his prime. And he helped transform Andy Robertson into a force on Liverpool's left side.

Klopp's style helps to elevate all the members of his squad - not just the most talented.

Fitness and mental readiness are highly important, and some newcomers might just have that to impress the new manager.

But man-marking is prevalent in Germany's top flight, while Klopp prefers his teams to close down the player in possession to create superior numbers around the ball. So some of the Bundesliga players will have to adapt quickly.

"It is not important who plays but how someone plays," Klopp said last week. "I expect a lot from the beginning. It could be a bit wild, but I accept that. It just has to be lively."

Klopp has chosen younger squads compared to the ones we saw in the past couple of years. Manuel Neuer, Antonio Rudiger and Pascal Gross have retired from international football, and other 30-somethings might just not receive a chance to get into the team again.

"I think it is about time to wish the new generation best of luck," Gross said after Brighton's win over Arsenal on Saturday. "I still enjoy playing football here in the club, but there's a change in Germany and rightfully so."

Both squads for this international break have an average age between 24 and 25. Youth and energy seem to be preferred.

"I have the desire to work with guys who cannot wait to wear this jersey, who want to play the kind of football everybody enjoys and who perform even better wearing the national team jersey," Klopp said.

We can expect from him to simplify Germany's approach to ball possession. Predecessor Julian Nagelsmann bent over backwards to hide some of the flaws he detected in his squad and thus created highly complex tactical systems.

On the contrary, Klopp intends to put an emphasis on the wings and break defences there. We saw what he was able to achieve with the likes of Mohamed Salah, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Sadio Mane from wide areas.

While underwhelming at the past couple of international tournaments, Germany still possess a deep talent pool. Cologne's rising star Said El Mala and 18-year-old Bayern Munich talent Lennart Karl will get chances to show their skills on the wings.

Freiburg's Derry Scherhant and Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi provide plenty of speed, just like Brentford's Kevin Schade who has returned to the squad after being left out for the World Cup. There is potential for an exciting Germany side we have not seen in quite a while.

Finally, the emotional component plays a role in Klopp's entire approach. He works towards a fresh start for the national team and a new spirit in the country.

Last Thursday, he wore a cap that read "One of 83 million". It was a clear indication he wants to unite all 83 million Germans behind this team and they are all in it together.

Klopp has spent plenty of time thus far attempting to shape narratives off the field - but now the spotlight turns to his ability to get the best out of his group of players on the pitch.

articles.summary: Chelsea, Bayern Múnich, Benfica, Mónaco o Sporting de Portugal se interesan por Adama Jeng, el mediocentro defensivo de futuro
articles.body: Los grandes equipos de Europa están pujando para fichar al niño prodigio Adama Jeng, un joven talento gambiano de 15 años que es considerado una de la mayores promesas de África. El centrocampista, que ya mide 1, 88 m., ha destacado con la selección sub-17 de Gambia durante el torneo sub-17 de la zona A de la WAFU (Unión de Fútbol de África Occidental). Adama Jeng fue uno de los jugadores más destacados de los 'Baby Scorpions', que se proclamaron campeones ganando en los penaltis a Senegal. El 'Daily Mail' informa que grandes de Europa como Chelsea, Bayern Múnich, Benfica, Mónaco o Sporting de Portugal han empezado la carrera para fichar el emergente mediocentro defensivo, que se ha formado en la cantera del Samger FC que cumplirá los 16 años en diciembre de 2026.
